extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, patent attorneys/agents, USPTO OED staff, and attorneys facing USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing USPTO disciplinary investigations, service, practitioner duties under the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct, default judgment practice, and factors for sanctions (including exclusion and reinstatement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of Complaint and Methods of Service (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2) and § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Service on a respondent in a USPTO disciplinary proceeding may be completed by mailing a copy of the Complaint by any delivery service that provides confirmation of delivery or attempted delivery to a respondent who is a registered practitioner at the address provided to OED pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.11; when it is unclear whether the respondent received the Complaint, service by publication in the USPTO Official Gazette pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b) may be used (publication for two consecutive weeks, with thirty days from the date of publication of the second Notice to file an Answer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the decision: certified mail to addresses of record, process server attempts, email notifications, and eventual service by publication (Official Gazette notices on consecutive weeks); publication starts a 30-day deadline from the second notice. Practice note: use delivery services that provide confirmation of delivery/attempted delivery; if receipt/signature is illegible or uncertain, supplemental measures (publication) may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner Duty to Maintain and Update Address of Record (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner must notify the OED Director of the postal address for the practitioner’s office and must provide written notice of any address change within 30 days of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to maintain an accurate correspondence address can lead to returned mail and may affect service of process; the Office directs correspondence to the address of record unless a different 'fee address' is designated for maintenance-fee notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to File an Answer and Consequences of Failure (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent is required to file a written Answer within the time prescribed; failure to timely file an Answer constitutes an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific timeframes in the decision: Complaint expected within 30 days; Notice of Docketing set a deadline (example: on or before Oct 17, 2022); publication-based service creates a 30-day deadline from the date of the second Official Gazette notice. Consequence demonstrated: respondent’s failure to answer led to being deemed in DEFAULT and admission of all allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for Default Judgment Procedure and Response Time (37 C.F.R. § 11.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: An OED Director may file a Motion for Default Judgment when respondent fails to answer; the respondent has a set period to respond to the motion (21 days under § 11.43 in this decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no response is filed within the prescribed time (e.g., no response by March 23 when motion filed March 2), the Court may grant default judgment. Prior USPTO decisions are cited where default was granted for failure to answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof in Disciplinary Proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although default may admit allegations, ordinarily OED must meet the clear-and-convincing standard to establish violations in contested proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Authority and Required Procedural Protections (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32; 37 C.F.R. part 11; 5 U.S.C. § 556)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admission and to suspend or exclude practitioners; disciplinary action under 35 U.S.C. § 32 requires notice and opportunity for hearing; disciplinary hearings are conducted per 37 C.F.R. part 11 (subpart C) and APA section 7 (5 U.S.C. § 556) by an authorized hearing officer (ALJ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites statutory authority for USPTO rulemaking and discipline; procedural safeguards (notice, hearing) must be preserved in discipline cases. ALJs may be appointed to hear USPTO disciplinary cases under interagency agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee Responsibility for Payment of Maintenance Fees (MPEP § 2504; § 2575; 37 C.F.R. § 1.20(e)-(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Holders of utility patents must pay maintenance fees to maintain a patent beyond 4, 8, and 12 years after grant; the Office has no duty to notify patentees when maintenance fees are due—responsibility rests with the patentee (or their agents). Communications about payments are generally directed to the correspondence address used during prosecution unless a separate 'fee address' is designated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: a practitioner of record who receives USPTO reminders is expected to notify the client; failure to do so can result in client harm (patents expiring) and disciplinary consequences. The decision uses MPEP citations to explain why the practitioner's failure to notify client of fee reminders was misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Abide by Client Objectives and Consult (37 C.F.R. § 11.102(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must abide by a client’s decisions concerning the objectives of representation and consult with the client as to the means by which those objectives are to be pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to inform a client that maintenance fees were due—and thus allowing patents to expire contrary to the client’s objectives—constitutes a violation of § 11.102(a). Evidence of petitions to revive after expiration showed the client’s objective was not to allow expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of Diligence and Promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must exercise reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not advising a client about upcoming maintenance fees or of patent lapse was held to violate § 11.103 (cited precedents: In re Valadares). The decision treats failure to notify and failure to act as lack of reasonable diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Keep Client Informed and Explain (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must keep clients reasonably informed about the status of matters and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to notify client of fee reminders or patent expiration violated these duties; cited precedents support that such omissions breach § 11.104.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Protect Client’s Interests After Termination (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: After termination of representation, a practitioner must take reasonably practicable steps to protect the client’s interests, such as surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled and cooperating with successor counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to respond to successor counsel’s requests for documents and explanations supporting petitions to revive patents violates § 11.116(d). The decision cites In re Gilboy as precedent: requiring client to hire other counsel due to a practitioner's failure to carry out services is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Cooperate with OED Investigations and Prejudice to Administration of Justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) and § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have a duty to cooperate with OED investigations; failure to cooperate is prejudicial to the administration of justice and undermines the integrity of the disciplinary system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision finds violation where respondent failed to respond to RFIs and Lack of Response letters sent by certified mail and emailed requests; failure to cooperate is an aggravating factor and may justify severe sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning Factors for Discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b); ABA STANDARDS)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining sanctions, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors. The decision also references the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions (STANDARDS) for aggravating/mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court applied these four factors and identified aggravating factors (bad faith obstruction, substantial experience) and a single mitigating factor (absence of prior disciplinary record). The primary purpose of discipline is protection of the public and administration of justice (STANDARDS § 1.1). Examples of cited aggravating/mitigating categories: STANDARDS §§ 9.1, 9.22(e),(i), 9.32(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and Mitigating Factors (examples and application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors may include bad-faith obstruction of proceedings (e.g., willful failure to participate) and substantial experience in the practice of law; mitigating factors include absence of a prior disciplinary record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats willful non-participation in investigations/proceedings as bad-faith obstruction (STANDARDS § 9.22(e)) and counts long practice history as aggravating (STANDARDS § 9.22(i)). While absence of prior discipline (STANDARDS § 9.32(a)) is mitigating, it may be outweighed by aggravation and harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of Mental State (intentional, knowing, negligent; willfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer’s mental state is assessed to determine culpability: intentional or knowing conduct is sanctioned more severely than negligent conduct; willfulness denotes conduct beyond mere negligence (knowledge or reckless disregard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision relied on admitted facts (default/admission) and cited cases (e.g., McLaughlin; Safeco) and STANDARDS § 3.0 to find respondent’s conduct knowing/willful based on failures to act and to respond to OED. Mens rea affects severity of sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Assessment in Sanctioning (actual or potential injury)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's conduct is a factor in determining sanctions; harm need not be established to find a violation but is relevant to the sanction's severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here, actual harm included three patents expiring and resultant loss of IP rights for years, plus costs for successor counsel and petitions to revive—used to justify severe sanction (exclusion). The decision notes harm increases severity and supports exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion from Practice and Reinstatement Eligibility (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60(b), 11.55 appeal rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions may include exclusion from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters; an excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of exclusion, conditioned on full compliance with rules for suspended/excluded practitioners (e.g., § 11.58). Appeals to the USPTO Director are available within thirty days (37 C.F.R. § 11.55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision ordered exclusion and referenced respondent’s responsibilities under § 11.58, the five-year earliest eligibility for reinstatement under § 11.60(b), and appeal rights (30 days to appeal to USPTO Director under § 11.55). Practical note: exclusion prevents practice before USPTO and reinstatement requires demonstrating rehabilitation and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Default/Admission on Findings of Fact and Mens Rea
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent fails to answer and is found in default, the respondent is deemed to have admitted the allegations; the court will set forth findings of fact based on those admitted allegations and may treat admitted allegations (including assertions of willfulness) as support for mens rea findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the decision, respondent’s absence produced admissions used to find willful misconduct, which informed the choice of exclusion as sanction. Prior USPTO decisions treat default admissions similarly.
